Think of it like this. Imagine you're reading a Dr. Seuss book about a bunch of beasts living on an island. There are two kinds of beasts: Fleetches and Flootches. Though the two are functionally identical in terms of intellect and general competence, Fleetches are in charge of pretty much everything. They hold the majority of political positions, they make the most money (beast-bucks!), they dominate the beast media, they enact all kinds of laws infringing on the bodily autonomy of Flootches. Individually, most of them are perfectly nice beasts, but collectively they benefit comfortably from inequalities that are historically entrenched in the power structure of Beast Island. So, from birth, even the most unfortunate Fleetches encounter fewer institutional roadblocks and greater opportunity than almost all Flootches, regardless of individual merit. One day, a group of Flootches get together and decide to agitate to change that system. They call their movement "Flootchism," because it is specifically intended to address problems that disproportionately disadvantage Flootches while benefiting Fleetches. That makes sense, right?

Now imagine that, in response, a bunch of Fleetches begin complaining that Flootchism doesn't address their needs, and they have problems too, and therefore the movement should really be renamed Beastism. To be fair. The problem with that name change is that it undermines the basic mission of the movement, because it obscures that beast society is inherently weighted against Flootches. It implies that all problems are just beast problems, and that all beasts suffer comparably, which cripples the very necessary effort to prioritize and repair problems that are Flootch-specific. Those problems are a priority because they harm all Flootches, systematically, whereas Fleetch problems merely harm individual Fleetches. To argue that all problems are just "beast problems" is to discredit the idea of inequality altogether. It is, in fact, insulting.

I understand that it was a multi layered system, and I did oversimplify it a little bit, but I just wanted to drive the point home that women have been voting for a very long time. I would have to challenge the notion that women were treated like property 100 years ago, though, at least in the UK, because while men were considered head of the house, it was kind of in name only. Sure, they represented their wife and family in the public sphere, and (in the case of the upper class) voted on behalf of their wives and children, but in the private sector, women pretty much made all the decisions in terms of housekeeping, and their husbands just had to respect it. Sargon actually has a great video where he reads through a marriage advice book from that period that was written by a woman, and was quite popular at the time.

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Ih-7F6czeds

As for the whole systematic oppression against women, as opposed to men, I challenge the notion that women were more oppressed than men, at least in the lower class, by the systems in place. In the upper class, I would say that men and women both had it pretty good, just in different areas. In the lower class, men were expected to work themselves to death in coal mines and die around the age of 30 to feed their families, as men were expected to be the breadwinner, something that disenfranchises men, especially during that period. Of course, there was a very chauvinistic attitude at the time and the education system was structured to teach men, so there were certainly issues for women to deal with.

Then there's the draft. The reasoning used to justify men voting on behalf of the family is because they were the only gender that could be conscripted during times of war, whereas women were not. When the suffragettes were fighting to have the vote extended to women while also maintaining that only men be eligible for the draft, and in fact protesting that all men be drafted and taking a strong part in the white feather campaign, was them having their cake and eating it too, and is one of the things I find objectionable about their activism at the time. Especially when they were trying to have men drafted that couldn't even vote. And, of course, war did come, the draft did come into play, and millions of men, against their own will, died some of the most horrible deaths imaginable. For reference:

From an emulation wiki:

  • Compatibility is lower than any modern emulator due to low accuracy to real SNES system. Games crashing - Der Langrisser (freezes after 2-3 hours), Super Mario RPG (freezes in many different points of the game), Star Ocean and many other games have freezing and crashing issues.

  • Bad sound emulation - A ton of games sound terrible on ZSNES; Earthworm Jim 2 has no sound effects.

  • Many of the co-processors, which are actually on the cartridges, are emulated in extremely strange ways. For example, Super FX for example is not clocked correctly - Star Fox runs twice as fast as it should.

  • Transparency - Kirby Dreamland 3, Mecarobot Golf, Jurassic Park and any game that uses pseudo hi-res translucency won't display correctly in the default graphics engine. To get them to display properly in 1.51, you have to press 8 to switch to the old graphics engine. Or use an older version.

  • Netplay was removed in 1.50.

I've never had any of those problems. Like, at all. It's never frozen on me, everything sounds perfect, and I just played Star Fox a few weeks ago with no issues. I'm not saying none of this has ever happened to you, but my own personal experience with ZSNES has been nothing but positive.

There is a good reason why we have cryptographers, scientists, physicists, mathematicians, scholars, engineers and other highly qualified professionals who understand the dangers of inserting backdoors into crypto, and who can explain very clearly that there is no such thing as only the good guys having access to backdoors. If a backdoor is wired into any product, be it software or hardware, everyone has access to it. From that point on, it is only a matter of time in the race of who can break in first.

Notice that it is not extremists, terrorists, criminals and other individuals of dubious character protesting online against crypto backdoors. It is law-abiding, educated scholars. Will someone--anyone--with a law enforcement badge bother to listen? Or are they just going to stick their fingers in their ears, close their eyes, and scream "bad guys" and "dark places"? You cannot win this argument with demagoguery, rhetoric, fear-mongering, innuendo, FUD, sensationalism, gossip or propaganda. None of those tactics will invalidate sound science.

A badge will not automatically give anyone a degree or a thorough understanding of all the science disciplines involved in cryptography. However, we understand your concern. Please hold; a highly qualified and well-trained scientist will be with you in a moment to walk you through the issue, at no cost to you. Thank you for your patience, and thank you for choosing reason over FUD.
